title: Forbes Insights: How Advanced Technology Is Creating New Possibilities, And Requirements, For Financial Reporting And Audit
text:
By Jeff Koyen
Technology continues to change how companies manage their finance function, and most executives are fully aware—and supportive—of tech’s role within their organizations. But precisely what benefits does technology bring today, how will this change in coming years and in what ways will tech influence the next generation of finance professionals?
These questions were at the heart of Forbes Insights’ May-June 2021 survey of 250 senior U.S. finance executives, performed in conjunction with KPMG LLP. The executives represent all major sectors and work at organizations posting at least $1 billion in global revenue for the most recent fiscal year. We also spoke with several leaders at KPMG to lend greater context to the data.
What do executives expect from their technology?
“Companies are constantly looking for greater insights related to their business,” says Heather Paquette, national technology assurance leader, KPMG. “Leveraging smart analytics and artificial intelligence gives them those insights, both to generate business value and make financial decisions.”
Smart analytics and artificial intelligence—throw in cloud computing, and you’ve got what might be considered the Dream Team of finance technology. Edge computing, blockchain and automation technologies, such as robotic process automation (RPA) and business process automation (BPA), are also playing important roles.
Which solutions will achieve mainstream adoption in the industry the soonest, and how will expectations change as a result?
Which Technologies—And Why
As the survey demonstrates, finance executives are well aware that artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies are being used in their industry. And since it’s as expensive as it is powerful, the latest finance tech must justify itself practically.
The most obvious benefit for executives is getting better insights through more nuanced data. As Scott Flynn, KPMG’s vice chair, Audit, says, “In the conversations I have with C-suite executives ... that’s the thing they’re looking for: the insights that the data is able to identify.”
In terms of specific must-haves for their internal finance functions right now, most executives pointed to cloud computing and storage (74%); smart analytics, including data extraction and transformation and data visualization (62%); and artificial intelligence, which includes machine learning and natural language processing (56%).
Most executives expect BPA (43%), process mining technology (42%) and RPA (48%) to be required finance capabilities within two years.
“Robotic process automation is undervalued at this time,” Paquette says. “It should be higher on executives’ radars.”
Many executives expect blockchain (51%) and edge computing (36%) to become important internal tools within five years—but no sooner than three.
Internal Functions Versus External Auditors
For most business leaders, internal reporting is just one facet of the finance function. The role of the external auditor is often just as important, as is that auditor’s use of the latest digital tools.
Nearly all executives (98%) said their external firm uses advanced technology in the audit process, and most agree this improves the quality of the audit (98%). (This represents a marked change from just three years ago, when 74% of executives noted the use of advanced tech by external auditors. Digging deeper, just 26% of executives in 2018 considered artificial intelligence a must-have for outside firms; today that figure is 61%.)
Using advanced technology, executives say, delivers deeper insights into areas of heightened risk, provides better benchmarking and increases data coverage.
The majority of executives also say advanced technology enhances their client experience (94%).
Perhaps that’s why most executives (58%) see external auditors as being more technologically advanced than internal finance functions. Just 8% of executives believe their own use of tech is more advanced.
These results don’t surprise Flynn.
“We’ve got to be able to prepare, perform and execute against audits for companies across a wide spectrum,” he says. “It’s moving with them, but [also] anticipating where they're going.”
While he agrees with Flynn’s assessment, Christian Peo, national managing partner, Audit Quality and Professional Practice, KPMG, believes it equally important to pay close attention to that minority of finance executives on the technological vanguard.
“To keep up with those 8% who are changing and innovating so rapidly, we need to invest and spend time and be on par with how they’re changing,” Peo says. “We need to keep up with them, and we need to spend—that’s an opportunity to enhance audit quality.”
Where, then, should external auditors be investing in order to keep current and deliver on these heightened expectations?
“Data and analytics,” says Paquette. “Sixty to seventy percent of controls expect to be automated in the next five to 10 years. ... We’re also evolving our audit approach along with the companies that we audit.”
The Future Of Talent
Conversations about AI and automation often center on the risk to human jobs: Will robots replace people? The answer, of course, is “No.” Automation will change how many industries operate, but the “human factor” will prove irreplaceable in certain functions.
For finance, Flynn says, “Those people who are intellectually curious and are able to draw insights from disparate data pools, those people are going to be truly exceptional. … There’s a role for them in audit’s future and, candidly, finance in the future.”
Flynn believes that technology will change financial reporting in ways that improve the lives of finance professionals, auditors included. In the form of machine learning and natural language processing, for example, AI can automate tasks that require time-consuming manual oversight. As AI adoption grows, more of the industry’s human capital can be dedicated to more creative tasks.
Seen through this lens, it makes sense that tomorrow’s finance professionals will be expected to be sharp, insightful thinkers. Most executives say their financial reporting staff must have critical thinking, reasoning and problem-solving skills (80%); investigative financial skills (66%); and an ability to achieve specific objectives by developing relevant data analytics (66%).
“The ability to perform in-depth analysis and draw correlations from distinct data is going to be really important,” says Flynn. But, he adds, it “goes without saying” that fluency with technology will be important as well.
Indeed, the jobs of next-gen auditors may be more technical in nature than those of their peers working in internal finance functions. For the former, our executives prioritized fluency with AI, RPA and blockchain (76%) and a background in data science (75%).
“Whether it’s data and analytics or using bots in auditing procedures, we believe the next generation of auditors must have foundational skills in technology,” says Paquette, “and they must acutely understand the financial processes and that intersection of risk between financial and technology.”
Though he agrees that technical proficiency is vital to the rising generation of financial professionals, Peo offers one important caveat: “[T]hey also need the traditional skills: being able to speak with management [and] the audit committee in a way that’s understandable, take very detailed findings that are uncovered through the use of technology and put it in a way that’s understandable in nonaudit speak.”
The “human touch” will never become obsolete.
Toward Greater Automation
For good reason, digital transformation is an ongoing concern among most executives. As the survey reveals, finance technology is evolving quickly and bringing change to the industry.
Trends toward greater automation are apparent, as are preferences for technology that produces greater insights. Executives are putting great demands on their own organizations to remain technologically current, which in turn puts more pressure on their external auditors.
This is the future, says Paquette.
Executives want to optimize and “digitize their business holistically,” she says. “Those trends are going to continue to increase, both in driving business transformation [and] driving automation of the auditors.”
Jeff Koyen is an award-winning journalist, media entrepreneur and early cryptocurrency investor. He lives in Curaçao with his family.
The views and opinions expressed herein are those of the survey respondents and do not necessarily represent the views and opinions of KPMG LLP.

title: AI and maths to play bigger role in global diplomacy, says expert
text:
International diplomacy has traditionally relied on bargaining power, covert channels of communication and personal chemistry between leaders. But a new era is upon us in which the dispassionate insights of AI algorithms and mathematical techniques such as game theory will play a growing role in deals struck between nations, according to the co-founder of the world’s first centre for science in diplomacy.
Michael Ambühl, a professor of negotiation and conflict management and former chief Swiss-EU negotiator, said that recent advances in AI and machine learning mean that these technologies now have a meaningful part to play in international diplomacy, including at the Cop26 summit later this month and in post-Brexit deals on trade and immigration.
“These technologies are partially already used and it will be the intention to use them more,” said Ambühl. “Everything around data science, artificial intelligence, machine learning … we want to see how can it be made beneficial for multilateral or bilateral diplomacy.”
The use of AI in international negotiations is at an early stage, he said, citing the use of machine learning to assess the integrity of data and detect fake news to ensure the diplomatic process has reliable foundations. In the future these technologies could be used to identify patterns in economic data underpinning free trade deals and help standardise some aspects of negotiations.
The Lab for Science in Diplomacy, a collaboration between ETH Zürich where Ambühl is based and the University of Geneva, will also focus on “negotiation engineering”, where existing mathematical techniques such as game theory are used either to help frame a discussion, or to play out different scenarios before engaging in talks.
These tools are not new. Game theory was developed in the 1920s by the Hungarian-American mathematician, John Von Neumann, initially to formalise the concept of “bluffing” in poker and later used to weigh up various nuclear strike scenarios during the cold war. However, until recently such techniques fell out of mainstream use “not due to a lack of technology but rather a lack of knowledge,” according to Ambühl. “Diplomats are not that accustomed to it.”
But as the world becomes more tech and data-savvy, those who ignore quantitative methods risk selling themselves short. Ambühl said that, as Switzerland’s chief EU negotiator, he ran a game theory simulation ahead of talks that led to Switzerland joining the Shengen area and a raft of agreements with the EU on tax, trade and security. The analysis indicated that it was in Switzerland’s interest for the negotiations to take place as a package rather than sequentially, and so Swiss government insisted on this as a basis for talks.
Did the EU do their own analysis? “I don’t think so,” said Ambühl. “We didn’t tell them that we did game theory.”
Taking a mathematical approach can also help “de-emotionalise” underlying conflicts, according to Ambühl. He cites talks between Iran and the P5+1 countries in Geneva in 2005, where as facilitator he came up with a mathematical formula for the rate at which Iran would reduce its number of nuclear centrifuges. “When we presented the idea it was ‘Now let’s talk about the size of this gradient, alpha, which is between 0 and 1’,” he said. “You discuss it on a more technical level.”
Can deep-rooted political issues really be distilled down into a gradient on a curve? Ambühl said that this misses the point, which is to crystallise what is under negotiation not to offer a fully-formed solution. “It’s not about making a technical agreement,” he said. “It’s a political question, but you break it down. You divide it into problems and sub-problems and sub-sub-problems.”
A more scientific approach does not mean ditching traditional methods. “I’m not pretending you can only negotiate well if you do it this way,” he said. “It still depends very much on other factors like how much bargaining power you have, whether you have a charming negotiator, whether you have a PM behind who supports tough negotiations and how well have you prepared.”
Are there risks that any of these new approaches could backfire, with rival AIs escalating conflicts or arriving at diplomatic solutions that are mathematically optimal, but have disastrous real-world consequences?
“You’re not going to war only because a blind algorithm decides it – it goes without saying that this would be idiotic,” said Ambühl. “It’s always only a decision tool.”
“You cannot just blindly rely on it, but you also cannot blindly rely on the gut feeling of these politicians,” he added. “You have to make a clever combination of new technologies and the political analysis.”

title: Council Post: Embrace The Era Of Change And Evolution With Self-Learning AI
text:
Co-founder & CEO of TheMathCompany.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has permeated almost every area of our lives, and this is good news. From voice assistants that process and understand natural language to technology that reminds us to restock vegetables in the refrigerator, the wide reach of AI has made our lives easier, simpler and better.
In truth, this is simply a ripple effect of several startups and multibillion-dollar companies diving headfirst into AI-augmented technology and unlocking its transformative capacity over the past decade. From facial recognition to smart farming, cybersecurity and personalized shopping, AI has come a long way since its inception and has now evolved into its inevitable next form: self-learning AI.
Self-learning AI recognizes patterns, learns from data and becomes more intelligent over time — having gone from being a mere possibility to a reality, to the next significant capability for businesses. This technology has particularly found its footing among automotive manufacturers, with its wide adoption standing testament to its increasing accuracy, reliance and intelligence.
For instance, autopilot cars are equipped with robust planning and decision-making systems that can navigate through real-world, complicated and uncertain scenarios. They are equipped to change lanes and optimize routes, steering clear of traffic while also navigating to desired destinations. The integrated AI capabilities leveraged by these vehicles stream data from multiple cameras and sensors to automate several processes, from object detection to parking, with little human intervention.
Interestingly, the three cogs that have accelerated this maturation of self-learning AI are multitasking, meta-reasoning and meta-learning, which enable learning from one activity to drive another, strategic thinking and learning to learn, respectively. While research continues on how AI can be modeled on the human brain and the beginnings of self-learning technologies are already in play in real-world contexts, AI is poised to play a bigger role in the future.
Self-learning AI is the inevitable next step, and businesses are already using its transformative capacity, integrating intelligent capabilities into existing infrastructure. Let's dive into three industries that have unlocked immense value from self-learning AI technology.
AI-Enabled Diagnoses in Healthcare
With Covid-19 pushing healthcare infrastructure to and beyond its limits, several global healthcare systems have adopted AI capabilities to bring agility to processes and ensure timely patient care. According to a Gartner, Inc. report, self-learning algorithms are now being used to support rapid diagnoses, with AI-based CT image interpretation systems developed to monitor disease progression as well as identify and alert abnormalities on chest X-rays. AI-based decision support tools are also being designed to bolster diagnoses by accounting for patients' age, vital signs and presence of chronic conditions — with these tools demonstrating up to 95.5% accuracy in some cases.
Gauging Creditworthiness Driven By AI in Banking and Financial Services
Fintech has significantly impacted banking and financial services, changing the face of the industry entirely. Statista notes that between 2010 and 2019, the total value of investments in fintech increased, reaching an all-time high of $215.4 billion. The Financial Stability Board also highlights how credit scoring has now become an increasingly machine learning (ML)- and AI-driven endeavor, speeding up lending processes while limiting incremental risks. In the past, transactional data and payment history acted as the foundation for credit scoring. However, with advanced self-learning models integrated into technological ecosystems, this process has changed vastly.
To capture a nuanced view of the creditworthiness of customers, self-learning AI models are analyzing structured, unstructured and semi-structured data — including social media activity, pay stubs, mortgage forms, tax documents and so on. The insights unearthed from this constellation of data are helping assess behavior and willingness to pay (WTP), which has further facilitated a faster and more cost-effective segmentation of borrower quality and credit scoring.
Minimizing Human Intervention in Supply Chain
The current economic climate warrants for supply chain networks to be purpose-driven through digital interconnectedness and supported by innovative technologies. In this regard, hyperautomation is growing in popularity — bolstered by self-learning AI capabilities that allow for interconnectedness between different applications, analyzing vast amounts of data and autonomously performing tasks that previously required human judgment. This involves a combination of robotic process automation (RPA), ML and AI, helping automate transactional processes, complex decision-making and so on while supporting the growth of an autonomous supply chain.
For instance, RPA can automatically monitor inventory and notify managers of dips in the inventory below demand levels, thereby mitigating risks, decreasing costs and improving productivity by 40% to 60%. These capabilities stem from self-learning AI models that scan through trillions of real-time data to process and allow for the quick generation of insightful information, such as demand forecasts and changes in consumer behavior.
Despite all these advancements, what we are witnessing is merely the nascency of self-learning AI; from addressing limitations in training datasets to eliminating harmful emissions and enabling transfer learning between applications, the possibilities are truly endless. With the growth of industries augmented by self-learning AI, businesses — now more than ever — can benefit from an open and agile mindset and a culture that strives to revolutionize existing solutions, unlocking opportunities in helming a bold new future.

title: Council Post: Finding The Data: How To Avoid AI And Analytics Project Failures
text:
Ajith Sankaran, Senior Vice President, Course5 Intelligence.
The pace of digital transformation has accelerated, and there is no longer any question as to the massive impact rapid digitization driven by AI and data analytics has had on our world.
While many organizations are reaping the benefits of successful AI and analytics implementations, the reality is that many of these projects continue to under-deliver or even fail. This is despite all the advances in supporting technologies and the ever-increasing investments poured into the industry. Back in 2018, Gartner made a widely shared prediction that 85% of AI projects would eventually fail. Fast forward to the current day and these estimates have remained; in fact, analysts and industry leaders have continued to make similar predictions along the way.
Failures In Data
These failures and challenges have been attributed to reasons such as lack of a cohesive AI strategy, application of AI and analytics to the wrong projects, poor organizational alignments and lack of continued C-suite commitments. However, I believe that the single biggest reason for the failure of AI and analytics projects involves data. I see data failures manifesting in the following ways:
• Absence Of Data Strategy And Data Governance: While companies develop grand AI and analytics road maps, some fail to build a data strategy and set up data governance systems. If this foundation is not laid, it inevitably leads to multiple failure points.
• Challenges With Data Availability: Data silos are a reality, and there will always be multiple levels of dependencies when it comes to organizing data. Challenges emerge when there are delays in accessing and connecting with different data sources. Even if some of the cloud-native systems ensure easy data availability, integrating with legacy systems is a challenge that organizations continue to struggle with.
• Poor Data Quality: While the adage "garbage in garbage out" has become cliched, it remains a very real fact when it comes to challenges faced by organizations implementing AI and analytics. Clean, machine learning-ready data is a prerequisite for AI and analytics projects. Organizations often realize that the data they have is not clean only after they start ambitious programs.
• Lack Of Data Readiness: Even if the data is clean, it still needs to be ready or labeled for use by analytics, machine learning and AI algorithms. Unfortunately, without a sound data strategy, labeled data is often not available, and this affects the projects. In many cases, data scientists end up wasting their time and companies' resources labeling and annotating data.
• Low Levels Of Data Literacy: With increased usage and data democratization, everyone in the organization, not just the data scientists and data engineers, must understand and use data. In other words, they need to be data literate. According to a recent Harvard Business Review article, while 90% of business leaders cite data literacy as a key to company success, only 25% of employees feel confident in their data skills. A lack of data literacy can lead to data silos, data security challenges and low levels of inclusivity.
The Way Ahead
While these challenges remain, there is no question about the growing promise of AI and analytics projects. Overall, I see that success stories in this industry all have one common theme: a well-thought-out data strategy with robust data governance systems.
According to Gartner, within three years, "75% of organizations will shift from piloting to operationalizing AI." Many organizations have already realized the importance of a sound data strategy as well as the need for ensuring the availably of clean, analytics-ready data. Within your own operations, data engineering needs to be considered as necessary as data science and as a foundational element to the success of your AI and analytics programs.
I recommend organizations adopt data operations (DataOps) to drive enterprise-wide programs, and data engineering should play an integral role alongside data science. Utilizing DataOps can help enable better collaboration among data scientists, data engineers and other key stakeholders. This will ensure that every team is working in sync to use data more appropriately and more efficiently, which in turn leads to more accurate analysis, better insights and improved business strategies.

title: IBM Federated Learning Research - Extracting Machine Learning Models From Multiple Data Pools
text:
As machine learning becomes more pervasive in the data center and the cloud there will be a need to share and aggregate information and knowledge but without exposing or moving the underlying data. This is going to be especially true where there are multiple separate data silos that contain related information. There’s many different reason why related data is held in separate, smaller data pools and not in a unified larger data pool. The reasons could include multiple organizations trying to collaborate without moving the data, government regulatory compliance issues, geographic separations, privacy issues, or the data in each location could be proprietary.
There are situations where different enterprises cooperate in training a machine learning model for non-competitive reasons. For example, financial institutions may collaborate on data that prevents money laundering and fraud, and medical research facilities can work collaboratively on improving diagnostics and treatment. However, due to regulation, privacy requirements, and secrecy, financial firms will not share transaction data and medical institutions cannot share patient data. And yet using these different sources of data is still important to build ML models on large and representative training datasets.
One area of research into how to combine these separate pools is through federated learning (FL), a machine learning process where knowledge is extracted from the data where the data resides and then merged into a larger knowledge base. In this technique, multiple parties run machine learning training on isolated data without exposing data or sharing that data, and then the models are shared with an aggregator that merges the local models into a global model.
IBM is one of the companies researching systems for this form of federated training. I recently had a chance to talk with Heiko Ludwig, who is a principal research staff member and senior manager of AI platforms at IBM Research AI. We discussed the application and IBM's programs for federated learning.
IBM is interested in FL because it's going to be important for enterprise level AI. Enterprises often have multiple data silos and may have legal or geographic restrictions on sharing or moving data. Those restrictions could be governmental or agency such as consumer privacy acts and HIPAA compliance issues. There may also be trade secret information that companies do not want to share outside of a secure server or a customer requirement. In addition, moving massive amount of data for training has IT and communication costs and bandwidth issues as well.
The data may come from multiple sources such as robots, edge devices, medical data, cell phones, etc. Those sources of data may also come from unsupervised learning, where the data is not processed by data scientists, or they can be processed and labeled. The diversity of data makes blending knowledge extracted from local data pools complicated.
How does Federated Learning work?
In FL, each individual data pool is processed to create a machine learning model, just like normal ML training. The key difference is that an aggregator then queries each of the parties to obtain the information necessary to build a common predictive model, as seen in Figure 1.
Each of the party’s individual data set is used to train a model based solely on the local data. Each individual party then sends back a response with the requested ML weights, gradients, and sample counts. The aggregator then fuses the individual responses into a new model using a fusion algorithm. It is also the aggregator’s responsibility to determine whether all or enough parties have responded. If the individual parties are too numerous (like cell phones), it may be possible to subsample the individual parties by the aggregator. Then, the merged ML model data is sent back to all parties for the next round of training.
Figure 1. Federated Learning model
The ML networking structure may also be split in two different layers: those that are shared and those that are not shared (split learning). Likewise, the response from the aggregator may only update certain layers of the end models.
The most important thing is that raw data is never shared - only the ML model extracted from the data.
FL is still an active research topic and there are many different approaches. There are several challenges such as data set heterogeneity. The FL process could take many iterations of local training at the parties, transmission of the model to the aggregator, model fusion, and return of the fused model to the parties for more local training. It is essential that the transfer of model data between the parties and the aggregator is secure and reliable. This is another challenge that must be considered before deploying out a FL program.
In this model the aggregator is responsible for accumulating and merging of the data models, although theoretically it is possible that each individual peer could send data and integrate each individually, but this is more in the realm of research and not deployment because of its complexity. There’s also the opportunity to use FL to take pretrained models and the use the FL process to customize the models to the application for greater accuracy.
IBM’s Federated Learning Framework
IBM FL is built with a Python library designed to support the machine learning process in a distributed environment. It is also designed to ensure the easy implementation of new FL algorithms. The library contains an aggregator and a party client of each data pool as shown in Figure 2. It is a modular design that allows the framework to provide a communication infrastructure independently of the federated learning algorithm and the actual machine learning library that performs local training.
Figure 2. IBM FL Framework
The goal of the IBM FL framework is to allow data scientists and machine learning professionals to transition from existing practices of model development to building federated machine learning models. To be useful, the FL infrastructure must be easy to deploy by an enterprise and fit into regular IT infrastructures.
The goal of the community version enables researchers in federated learning to design novel FL algorithms and protocols that can be deployed and experimented on with ease.
Figure 3. The process of training a NN with IBM FL Framework
IBM has released a community version of its FL for research use. There are several features that are stripped out, but it provides the necessary functionality for research purposes and is supported with tutorials and a quick setup guide. There’s a beta version release on Cloud Pack for Data and the cloud.
Figure 4. IBM’s two offerings for FL Framework
Application Examples
The IBM FL platform can train on any data, but there’s a few initial market opportunities. It’s best used on areas where there’s connected devices and application silos. IBM’s first target application is the hybrid cloud environment where a company with a global footprint has data locked into separate silos due to regulatory requirements, geographic separation, or business practices. The purpose of IBM FL is to gather global intelligence from these localized data pools.
Another target application is the scenario where a group of companies need to collaborate. Examples here include financial institutions that need to collaborate on money laundering patterns and detection. The goal is to help all institutions, but without releasing confidential information. Oil companies can aggregate learning on demand prediction. In medicine, there was a study on sepsis in premature births that could be shared across countries and hospitals. This is one examples where research doctors from different university can share knowledge without sharing patient data. In these cases, the preferred aggregator is an independent 3rd party. The aggregation of safety and medical ML models may be required in the future in an effort to save lives.
Another application for FL is from industrial edge devices, such as robots, that capture local data, but cannot transmit the data set due to privacy or bandwidth issues. This could be included in a product’s life cycle where the individual learning is aggregated and rolled out for improved models. It is here that trust and security must be managed.
The uses of FL may also be extended to consumer devices. Here the end units must be considered untrusted clients with the option to opt in or out of participation. With consumer devices, there will likely need to be a sub-sample of the total number of devices to keep the process manageable.
Summary
IBM has an engagement plan for customers and researchers on FL. The future roadmap includes work on privacy and security. The research continues into fusion effectiveness, ML tiering, automation tools, and bias mitigation.
IBM offers two versions of IBM Federated Learning for users to try: IBM Federated Learning as part of Watson Studio and IBM Cloud Pak for Data, and the IBM Federated Learning: Community Edition.
Federated learning is an important tool for major global institutions and industries that need to collaborate on learning but have restrictions on data locality and movement. It will be a critical as the world moves from machine intelligence to collective intelligence. For more information see this IBM site.

title: Can Artificial Intelligence Help To Close The Financial Equality Gap For Women?
text:
Women in America are disproportionately under-served when it comes to financial products and services. They own less than 1% of the country’s wealth, and they hold even less of their own assets.
A new study from the UConn Women’s Center for Research found that women entrepreneurs need more access to credit, training, and capital – including investments – if they want to grow their businesses. That's where AI can help.
One of the fastest-growing markets in finance is financial management, where artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to make decisions for customers' investment portfolios. As women are statistically more risk-averse than men, AI makes it easier for them to manage their money and reduce these risks.
Women who use an AI-assisted portfolio management service save on average $7000 per year over those who do not. Additionally, the chance that any given woman will experience poverty after retirement has decreased by 40% since 2000 due to saving just 10% of her paycheck each month into a 401(k).
How can women can build wealth utilizing advanced technologies and what should they should consider when looking at different services available on the market today?
Using AI to analyze your income and expenses regularly is a great way to help you better understand where your money goes each month. Most modern financial institutions have apps that will automatically categorize your spending into expense types, making it easy for you to see how much of your paycheck ends up going toward rent/mortgage, food, transportation, entertainment, etc.
Technology is empowering women to build wealth through AI-assisted financial management. Women are now able to invest and manage their finances by using technology that automatically invests and manages money for them. This software provides a unique algorithm for each woman with personalized goals, risk tolerance, income, and age.
AI software analyzes the data from bank account or credit card statements as well as her spending habits in order to make accurate recommendations about what she should do next financially. Technology has made it easier than ever for women who want to grow their own wealth without having to put time into investing on their own every day.
Ellevest is a great example of AI-enabled wealth management aimed at increasing wealth among women. Some of the goals are not only building wealth but also saving for retirement or financial emergencies.
Ellevest was built with data from an employer survey, which found that women earn 97% less than men in the same roles over their careers and thus require aggressive investment strategies to give them a one-third higher return on their portfolios to achieve the same level of wealth.
Real estate investing is another example of where women are making strides in increasing wealth. A 2014 National Association of Realtors survey found that in the previous 12 months, 3.5 million single women purchased a home, a 37% increase from 2010 and a 64% increase from 2006.
One of the people making this happen is Lakeisha Marion, a passionate mentor, educator, and activist who has devoted her life to empowering African American women. Her Wealthy Women’s Winning Circle provides an all-female space where members can learn about financial literacy while also growing their confidence.
As a real estate investor, Marion helps Miami-located women accumulate wealth utilizing a combination of industry understanding as well as AI-enabled investing tools. AI-enabled real estate investing tools empower women to be able to understand the trends in the market, as well as how to utilize these tools to find the best deals.
“I want to help empower women financially so they can leave a lasting legacy for their families,” says Marion.
Investing in women as entrepreneurs is also an important part of the equation. AI can help women build wealth to invest in their own ventures, as well as efficiently seek funding from angel and institutional investors.
The American Express OPEN State of Women-Owned Business report found that women own more than 9.4 million companies and generate $1.9 trillion in revenue, and it's estimated that by 2020, the number of women-owned businesses will increase at twice the rate of all privately held firms.
One area where AI's impact will be felt most acutely concerns investment opportunities for women entrepreneurs who don't have equal access to funding. There are many reasons why this occurs including historically, women have less exposure and fewer investment opportunities; there are fewer women-owned venture capital firms; when they do make investments, men tend to favor companies run by other men.
AI venture capital tools enable women to connect with women-led funds, diversity-focused funds and analyze the historical record of a fund's portfolio diversity. Crunchbase is a perfect example of how this type of technology can help to make venture capital more accessible to marginalized founders. When you begin to utilize AI to bring more diversity to business owners, you are increasing the possibilities for everyone.
AI is also capable of providing much greater transparency during the early stages in a startup's life when information about them is scarce. This allows investors to make better decisions when evaluating potential investments, and ensure that their investments are diverse.
AI is not the only way to level the playing field, however. There are many small steps that can be taken to help women succeed in business. We need more training opportunities, mentorships , and funding for female-led businesses . We need a shift in mindset about who can run a business and be successful.
All these insights add up to one thing: A woman needs to make investing in herself a priority, and AI can help her do that.

Currently, Lips is building more inclusive Machine Learning and Contextual AI technologies that can be used across industries to improve the online experience of traditionally marginalized communities.

title: Can AI Help Prevent Natural Disasters?
text:
Advanced analytics and other AI-driven tools and technologies have been transforming the way organizations function by harnessing valuable information from the largest datasets and providing important insights. With the continued growth of cognitive technologies and increasingly widespread adoption by many industries, what will the future of advanced analytics and AI adoption look like?
With the evolution of big data analytics over the past few years, the opportunities to apply this knowledge and to see how different industries are embracing AI and ML has shown tremendous value. However, the evolution and future of analytics doesn’t come without challenges. In a recent AI Today podcast interview with Antonio Cotroneo, Director of Technical Content Strategy at OmniSci, spoke about these potential challenges as well as opportunities for industries. Antonio’s background is in helping organizations maximize their geospatial data, mapping technology, and spatial analyses for decision-making, so it would only make sense that he provide comprehensive details on how advanced analytics and AI are changing the game when applied to helping prevent natural disasters. Anthony will be presenting at an upcoming Data for AI community virtual event on October 28, 2021 where he will explore how geospatial companies like OmniSci can play an important role in understanding the factors, risks, and impacts of wildfires.
Evolving Big Data and Data Analytics
As new developments in cognitive technologies continue to be introduced, the role of data and data analytics, especially in big data, has been evolving as well. The biggest shift, Antonio notes, is in how the collective idea of AI, ML, big data, analytics, and visualization is moving towards a broader audience. Technologies that were traditionally used or understood only by hardcore practitioners such as data scientists or other AI practitioners are now moving to knowledge workers. As a result of this transition, people are beginning to see the impact of AI on their day-to-day activities, both in their work and home lives. Whether it be through new tools or downstream analytics services, individuals are able to use these advancements to inform their decisions in ways that were not possible or common before.
Antonio explains that a decade ago in the industry of Geographic Information Systems (GIS), the focus was mostly on making observations about what had happened or mapping out current states and creating visuals. This is still an important aspect, but the newer focus is now on taking additional steps to not only observe or orient, but being able to track and predict the trajectory of any phenomenon. In terms of the larger trends, the commodification or consumerization of AI and ML is beginning to impact a broader audience, which is when these technologies will really penetrate the marketplace even more, says Antonio.
AI Adoption and Usage across Industries
Artificial intelligence has become a frequent topic of conversation in almost every industry worldwide, but which industries are truly leading the adoption of these advancements? The industries that are embracing these technologies the most seem to be those that have embraced the waves of technological advancements in the past. The U federal government and specifically the military, for instance, are taking a large role in the research, development, and use of AI, and other industries such as the FinTech market are key drivers as well. The industries that have traditionally pushed the boundaries of our current understanding of these concepts are the ones that are building the initial practical examples of how they can be used and pushing us into the new emerging spaces. The automotive and manufacturing industries are other key examples, with the automation of factories and transportation leading to the ideas of connected cities and services. In some industries, however, the privacy or security of organizations keep these technologies and concepts behind closed doors, but the overall trend across markets is towards widespread adoption and shared knowledge.
The Growth of Advanced Analytics
Artificial intelligence and machine learning are part of the overall trend of deriving more insights from data and finding the patterns and applying tools that lessen the cognitive load on the human. Antonio believes the future of these advanced analytics is again in how we are going to be using AI and ML products in our daily lives, from a more personal or human perspective. Analytics are already being used in financial services for tasks such as predicting whether an individual will default or qualify for a loan. Virtual assistants are another example of how analytics are becoming more and more incorporated into our personal lives. As advanced analytics become more and more present in our routines, the future is less about the deep technical worker being the individual interfacing or building solutions, services, and applications, and more about the users being impacted and using AI, ML, and analytics to accomplish even ordinary tasks.
Impacts of AI, Ethical Frameworks, and the General Future of AI
In today’s world, there are many ethical AI frameworks issued by corporations, non-profits, governments, and industry groups. More often than not, however, these various frameworks exhibit little overlap and are each focused on only a small subset of the aspects of using AI in ethical ways. While most frameworks mention fairness, bias, and dignity to some degree, there are many other areas such as consent, disclosure, contestability, interpretability and explainability, governance, and ownership that are important aspects of responsible AI. These aspects contribute to why there can sometimes be discomfort in performing the kinds of analytics that are in demand today. Antonio explains that at OmniSci, teams are careful to choose data partners that are curating datasets in ethical ways and critically considering these types of frameworks. There have been situations where he and his teams have had to walk away from certain uncomfortable situations where harvesting data can cause sticky situations related to privacy and security. This is why working with data providers that strive for both quality and equitability simultaneously in generating datasets is important for presenting an accurate picture of the world and ultimately for producing good analytics.
The general future of AI, says Antonio, is when we will not even realize that it is there, when systems, governments, and organizations – all the different components of our culture – are going to be in some ways functioning off of AI and ML through means we will not even notice. In fact, we are already entering that stage, as many individuals may not even be aware of how AI and ML is affecting their lives today. As this growth continues, one important area of focus as a culture, as technologists, and as people in this space, is the continued push for broader research and critical thought around AI and ethics. There are already plenty of people working on the technical problems, building more efficient algorithms, better models; there is no absence of data. However, in order to properly use the data to produce valuable information, the focus should be placed on how to leverage AI responsibly and inclusively. For additional insights on this Anthony will be presenting at an upcoming Data for AI community virtual event on October 28, 2021 where he will explore how geospatial companies can play an important role in understanding the factors, risks, and impacts of wildfires and how data, advanced analytics, and AI are making an impact.
